MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
Happy to help, and a bit of nervousness is a good sign: it means you'll take your time.

## What "lippage" means
Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the tile next to it, so the floor isn't flush. You can feel it with bare feet or catch a toe on it, and it shows up as shadows along the joints.

It matters for your tiles in particular because long tiles like 30 × 60 cm are often very slightly bowed in the middle. If you stagger them in a half-and-half brick pattern, the high middle of one tile lines up with the low end of the next. That's why the tile shop probably mentioned it. Two fixes:
- Offset each row by **a third** of a tile rather than a half.
- Or use **tile levelling clips**, which pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets.

## Grout colour
For pale grey porcelain, choose a **mid-grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. It hides everyday dirt and still looks deliberate. Avoid white or very pale grout on a floor, because it shows grime within weeks.

A grout labelled **stain-resistant** or **mould-resistant** helps a lot in a bathroom. Epoxy grout is the most stain-proof, but it's harder to work with, so a good cement-based grout with stain resistance is the easier choice for a first job.

## Floor before or after the toilet?
**Floor first.** Tile the whole floor, cutting neatly around the soil pipe, then fit the toilet on top. That gives a cleaner finish, no awkward cuts around the toilet's curved base, and means a future toilet can be swapped without patching the floor.

## How many boxes
- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18 m², so you need **24 tiles**
- Plus 10%: 26.4, which rounds up to **27 tiles**
- At 8 per box, 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **buy 4 boxes** (32 tiles)

The 8 spare tiles are worth having. A staggered layout and cutting around the pipe will use some, and keeping one or two afterwards means you can replace a cracked tile years from now. Check that all the boxes have the **same batch number**, because colour can vary slightly between batches.

## Message to the neighbours
> Hi [names],
>
> Just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles on Saturday morning for our bathroom floor, so there'll be some noise from the cutter. I'll keep it to the morning and try to get it done as quickly as possible.
>
> Thank you so much for being patient with us, especially with the skip on the drive for the past fortnight. It should all be finished soon!
>
> Many thanks,
> [Your name], no. [X]

You could suggest a start time, say "from about 10 am", if you know it. Neighbours tend to appreciate that.

## Three tips for your first floor
1. **Dry-lay before you mix anything.** Lay the tiles out loose with spacers to plan the layout. Start from the centre of the room or the doorway, the edge people see most, so the cuts at the walls are balanced and not thin slivers. Mark your lines in pencil.
2. **Prepare the subfloor properly.** It needs to be clean, flat and rigid, and primed if the adhesive instructions say so. Problems underneath show up as cracked tiles or grout later, and no amount of careful laying fixes them.
3. **Work in small batches and check as you go.** Mix only as much adhesive as you can use in about 20–30 minutes. For tiles this size, use a 10 mm notched trowel and also spread a thin layer on the back of each tile (back-buttering). Lift the occasional tile to check it's fully covered underneath, and run a straight edge across tiles to catch lippage while you can still adjust. Then keep off the floor for at least 24 hours before grouting.

The videos make it look easy because the people in them have done it hundreds of times. Going slowly is fine, and with careful preparation the floor should turn out well. Good luck!
